title: When, Where, and Why: Hierarchical Causal Explainability for Video Face Understanding with MLLMs

paper.title:
When, Where, and Why: Hierarchical Causal Explainability
for Video Face Understanding with MLLMs
paper.abstract:
Abstract Understanding facial behaviour in video requires answering three fundamental questions: when a key facial expression occurs, where the model attends on the face at that moment, and why that evidence is necessary rather than merely correlated. Today’s multimodal large
language models (MLLMs) can label and describe video, but they rarely provide faithful explanations,
especially for small facial movements that change over time. We present VideoFace-X-LLM , a framework for explainable facial video understanding comprising two key components. First, we introduce ExplainFace , a weakly supervised video-text corpus for facial behaviour understanding, automatically constructed from CelebV-HQ videos and validated through human evaluation and a two-model audit (at most 2.3% contradictions), demonstrating consistent gains across two backbone architectures. Second, H-TCC (Hierarchical Temporal Spatial Causal Concepts), which
finds the key temporal moments ( When ), the facial regions ( Where ), and verifies its causal necessity ( Why ) through targeted occlusion. Fine-tuning on ExplainFace
raises appearance Macro F1 from 19.48 % 19.48\% to 32.87 % 32.87\% ( + 13.39 +13.39 ), with gains of + 4.38 +4.38 on
actions, + 6.77 +6.77 on temporal emotion, and + 11.84 +11.84 F1 on deepfake detection. We also measure the explanations pointing lift, face/edge lift, stability, an Adebayo
sanity check, and a necessity test rather than only showing examples. Our models, code, and corpus are available on request for research use.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Faces in motion are one of the richest signals of human behaviour. A raised brow becomes surprise only when we see it change over time; a smile becomes warmth or sarcasm depending on the gaze, head motion, voice, and context around it. Such behaviour is temporal, multimodal, and causal: meaning comes not from single frames, but from how visual and audio signals change together. To understand it well, a model should answer three questions: when a key event happens, where it shows on the face at that moment, and why that region is needed and not just present by chance. The three are linked: a good explanation must find the right moment and region, then confirm that this evidence drives the output. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have improved fast on general vision language tasks, but they are still weak at fine-grained facial behaviour. Existing MLLMs [ 18 , 39 ] are trained on broad data and lack the priors needed to read small facial motions, micro-expression changes, and cues that depend on time but they remain strong at open-ended video description and soft-labeling. This is even harder for explanation, where a model must justify a prediction over time , not just describe a still image. Recent models such as InternVideo2.5 [ 38 ] , GPT-4o [ 26 ] , and Qwen3-VL [ 39 ] are strong at captioning, VQA, and general video analysis, yet they struggle with human-centric reasoning. Their training data is broad but thin on detailed labels for expressions, affect, body language, and temporal change. The real problem is not the models but the data: there is no large video-text dataset that describes faces in detail and lines up those descriptions with time. Weakly supervised, language-model-based dataset building has been tried for still images (for example FaceLLM’s FairFaceGPT [ 33 ] ), but not for video. Moving from images to video is harder, because it needs grounding of facial attributes in both space and time, plus reasoning over small changes that unfold over time. We address this with VideoFace-X-LLM , a model for explainable facial behaviour in video. We build ExplainFace , a weakly supervised video text corpus generated with Gemini [ 18 ] , giving time-aligned descriptions of facial attributes, expression dynamics, and audio visual context. To explain predictions, we introduce H-TCC (Hierarchical Temporal Spatial Causal Concepts), which finds when key events occur, where the model looks on the face, and why that evidence is needed, using hierarchical temporal saliency, spatial attribution, and a targeted occlusion test that confirms the identified evidence is necessary for the prediction. Importantly, fine-tuning on ExplainFace helps two different backbones, and we measure the explanations rather than only showing examples. Our main contributions are: • ExplainFace: a checked, weakly-labeled dataset. We label CelebV-HQ videos using Gemini instead of expensive frame-by-frame human labeling. We test how good these labels are with two human studies and a two-model check for bias, and show the labels still work well when used with two different model backbones. • H-TCC: a when/where/why framework that we actually measure. Every step of H-TCC is defined with clear equations, and we score the explanations with quantitative faithfulness metrics (pointing/face/edge lifts, stability, a sanity check, and a necessity test), not just example cases. • VideoFace-X-LLM. A video-understanding model for faces that explains its answers by pointing to the exact moments and regions that led to its decision.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: MLLMs for Vision Language Understanding. Recent MLLMs such as GPT-4o [ 26 ] , InternVideo2.5 [ 38 ] , LLaVA-NeXT [ 46 ] , and Qwen3-VL [ 39 ] have pushed general image and video reasoning, but lack the domain priors and time-aligned supervision needed for subtle facial behaviour, motivating our specialised corpus and adapted MLLM. Human-Centric Facial Behaviour Understanding. Many works apply MLLMs and foundation models to faces: recognition [ 13 ] , attribute analysis [ 23 ] , understanding [ 9 ] , and multimodal reasoning [ 11 ] . A recent survey [ 34 ] reviews how foundation models and LLMs are used for biometric security. Beyond CLIP, self-supervised methods learn facial representations, such as the masked-autoencoder MARLIN [ 8 ] , FaRL [ 49 ] , DINO-style distillation [ 6 ] , and ComFace [ 4 ] . Multi-task models [ 25 ] jointly do face parsing, landmarks, pose, and attributes. HumanOmni [ 47 ] uses a dedicated face branch and does well on expression and emotion. Still, no existing work gives both time-aligned video labels and clear, trustworthy explanations which is what VideoFace-X-LLM sets out to do. Bias and Explainability for Facial Behaviour Understanding. Facial datasets carry demographic imbalance that flows into predictions, with uneven results across gender, race, and age [ 14 ] . LLMs can amplify such bias when describing faces [ 17 ] , and bias checks for video face descriptions are still missing. 1) Temporal Explainability ( When ). Several methods [ 43 , 41 , 20 ] find key moments in video. TimeSuite [ 43 ] adds temporal grounding, SeViLA [ 41 ] picks keyframes, and VTimeLLM [ 20 ] and TimeChat [ 30 ] encode timestamps as text. Grounded-VideoLLM [ 36 ] splits video into spatial and temporal tokens. However, looking at only one time scale can miss events that overlap. 2) Spatial Explainability ( Where ). Grad-CAM [ 32 ] makes spatial heatmaps from gradients but does not suit transformer encoders or video. For vision transformers, attention rollout [ 1 ] traces information across layers, with refinements that mix gradients and attention [ 10 ] . GMAR [ 21 ] reweights heads by gradient importance, and LVLM-Interpret [ 35 ] extends rollout to large models. However, these maps do not line up with time. 3) Causal Validation ( Why ). Occlusion methods test whether evidence is needed by masking inputs and watching the output change. Zeiler and Fergus [ 42 ] used systematic occlusion for CNNs, RISE [ 28 ] uses random masks, and Fong and Vedaldi [ 16 ] frame it as finding the smallest change that flips the output. The problem is that they perturb blindly, without knowing when or where to look, which is slow and hard to read. They are also not built for video MLLMs, where masks must cover both time and space. Existing methods usually answer only one of when , where , or why , each with limits that our H-TCC addresses together.

sections.heading: 3 ExplainFace Corpus
sections.text: Most MLLMs [ 38 , 39 ] are trained on broad data with little human-centric detail, so they miss subtle facial behaviour and affect over time. We close this gap with ExplainFace , a video text corpus for detailed analysis of faces over time. We use videos from CelebV-HQ [ 50 ] and generate descriptions with the Gemini API [ 18 ] . The pipeline has two stages: a system prompt for video analysis (Prompt 3.1) followed by a multi-aspect description prompt; then a bias audit of those descriptions (Prompt 3.2). Fig. 1 shows the pipeline on the left.

sections.heading: 3.1 Prompting for ExplainFace Corpus
sections.text: System Prompt. Because the model can answer in different ways for different videos, we use a fixed system prompt (Prompt 3.1) so the output stays detailed and structured. Multi-Aspect Description Generation. For each video we generate descriptions over eight aspects: theme & narrative, visual elements, actions & movements, audio components, emotional tone, technical aspects, temporal flow, and context & relationships . These cover both still details and change over time. We use markdown headings so the format is consistent. Unlike FaceLLM [ 33 ] , which uses FairFace metadata to guide generation, we give Gemini no prior information about the video, because temporal content is hard to summarise in metadata. We let the model watch the video and extract the details itself. Prompt 3.1: System Prompt for Video Analysis System: You are an AI assistant specialized in analyzing video content with high accuracy and detail, suitable for multimodal video understanding and emotional analysis applications. Your task is to analyze and describe videos comprehensively, including visual elements, audio components, temporal dynamics, and emotional content. As an assistant, you should always analyze given video content thoroughly and provide objective, detailed descriptions based on observable information. Do not make assumptions beyond visible and audible traits. When analyzing a video, consider visual elements (scenes, objects, people, actions, lighting, camera movements, visual effects), audio components (speech, music, sound effects, ambient noise), temporal dynamics (sequence of events, transitions, pacing, duration), emotional expressions and behaviors (facial expressions, body language, vocal tone, emotional states), contextual information (setting, relationships between subjects, narrative flow), and technical aspects (video quality, editing techniques, production values). I may provide you with additional context about the video content, duration, or specific aspects to focus on. If you are asked for specific features or attributes, only describe what is asked in the question. Never say “I’m unable to analyze” instead, provide detailed descriptions based on the visual and auditory information available. Your answers should be comprehensive text descriptions (one or multiple paragraphs) that paint a clear picture of the video’s content and emotional landscape. Linking aspects to tasks. Each description aspect supervises a downstream task, as shown in Tab. 1 . For example, “Visual Elements” teaches appearance, “Actions” teaches action labels, and “Emotional Tone” teaches emotion and Action Units. This is why a general description corpus can train fine-grained facial tasks. Table 1 : How each ExplainFace description aspect supervises a downstream task. Description aspect Task it mainly supervises Visual Elements Appearance attributes Actions & Interaction Action recognition Emotional Tone & Expressions Emotion recognition, Action Units Temporal Flow Temporal emotion, deepfake (motion cues) Audio Components Multimodal context (speech, affect) Technical Aspects Manipulation / deepfake artifacts Quality Analysis for ExplainFace Corpus. AI-generated text can hallucinate, so we check the corpus with a ‘human-in-the-loop’ study. To test whether humans can match the AI descriptions to the videos, we ran two user studies with 10 10 participants who have computer-vision experience. User study 1 (Description quality): We randomly pick videos from the ExplainFace corpus and split them across 10 participants. After dropping incomplete answers, 531 pairs are left. Each participant gets the same instructions as Gemini and writes their own eight-aspect description, without seeing Gemini’s text. We then compare human and Gemini descriptions with semantic and lexical metrics. The goal is to check whether humans and Gemini describe the same content , not the same words. Semantic similarity is high while lexical overlap is low: SBERT averages 0.45 0.45 , against BLEU-1 0.06 0.06 and ROUGE-L 0.14 0.14 . For reference, two humans describing the same video reach only 0.38 0.38 , and a human and Gemini describing different videos 0.30 0.30 , so 0.45 0.45 exceeds both. This is exactly what we want: it shows humans and Gemini say the same thing in different words . Gemini writes longer, structured text; humans write short, informal notes. sections.heading: 3.2 Bias Analysis of ExplainFace Corpus
sections.text: MLLM descriptions can be biased, often through stereotypes or guesses from appearance [ 14 ] . So we add a bias-audit stage that checks each description. A separate prompt asks the model to flag biased language and suggest a neutral version grounded in what is visible. This makes the descriptions both detailed and objective. Subjectivity Audit. Descriptions can go beyond what is visible. A model might call a neutral face ‘reserved’ , or read ‘frustration’ from a raised brow. These are not wrong, but they are interpretations shaped by priors. To measure how much interpretive language is in ExplainFace, we use a two-stage audit. Stage 1: A prompt (Prompt 3.2) reviews each description with its video. For every interpretive statement, the model returns: (i) the exact phrase, (ii) why it goes beyond what is seen, and (iii) a more grounded alternative. If nothing is flagged, it says the description is purely observational. Example flagged pair. For one clip, the draft said the person “looks aggressive .” The audit flagged this as a guess about character and suggested “the brows are drawn together and the jaw is tense” - keeping the visible cue but dropping the assumption. Observations from Stage 1: We run the audit with two models: Gemini 2.5 Flash [ 18 ] and Qwen3-30B-Instruct [ 39 ] . Gemini calls about 70 % 70\% of descriptions observational and 30 % 30\% interpretive; Qwen3 calls about 60 % 60\% observational and 40 % 40\% interpretive. The gap shows the task is fuzzy: even two LLMs disagree on where observation ends and interpretation begins. This supports our view that objectivity in facial description is a spectrum, not a yes/no. Stage 2: Next we compare each flagged phrase with its suggested alternative. The two should keep the same meaning but change the framing. To test this, we use four metrics: i) Cosine similarity on MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings [ 37 ] ; ii) BERTScore [ 45 ] for meaning (should stay high); iii) BLEU [ 27 ] for word overlap (should drop if wording changed); and iv) NLI with DeBERTa [ 19 ] to label each pair as entailment, neutral, or contradiction (high entailment means the revision follows from the original). Prompt 3.2: Bias Analysis System: You are an AI ethics assistant. Review the following video and its accompanying text description for potential biases. Human: Does the description use stereotypical language related to gender, ethnicity, or age? Does it make unwarranted assumptions about emotion, intent, or character based on appearance? Your task is to: • Analyze both the video and the text description provided below. • Identify any specific phrases or sentences in the description that could be considered biased, stereotypical, or make unsupported assumptions. • For each identified statement, explain why it is potentially problematic. • Suggest a more neutral, objective alternative for each flagged statement, grounding your suggestion in observable facts from the video. If no biased statements are found, state that the description appears to be objective and free of bias. Your response must be structured using the exact following markdown headings: Overall Assessment (Provide a one-sentence summary of your findings.) Bias Analysis (If biased statements are identified, list each one as follows:) Problem Statement 1: [The exact quote from the description] Explanation 1: [Why it is potentially problematic] Suggested Alternative 1: [A more neutral, objective rephrasing] Final Conclusion (A brief concluding thought on the description’s overall objectivity.) When a flagged sentence is rewritten to be more objective, the meaning stays the same: BERTScore F1 is 0.93 0.93 for both Gemini and Qwen3. At the same time, BLEU is low ( 0.21 0.21 and 0.20 0.20 ), so the wording changed a lot but the meaning did not. The audit changes how something is said, not what is said. Contradiction rates are very low: only 2.3 % 2.3\% (Gemini) and 1.6 % 1.6\% (Qwen3), so over 97 % 97\% of pairs stay factually consistent. Reaching this at scale, with no human annotation, shows the corpus is robust. Neutral cases ( 43.9 % 43.9\% for Gemini, 61.5 % 61.5\% for Qwen3) are usually extra hedging or detail, not errors. The two auditors disagree on how much is subjective, yet they give almost the same similarity and contradiction numbers, so our conclusion does not depend on the auditor. Together, this shows ExplainFace is accurate and rich, and its interpretive language links low-level cues to human-level meaning. Final Conclusion: After the audit we keep the full corpus, including interpretive descriptions: facial behaviour is naturally subjective, and this interpretive layer matters for emotion and attribute prediction removing it would leave only anatomy. As our results show, these descriptions help rather than hurt.

sections.heading: 4 VideoFace-X-LLM
sections.text: We propose VideoFace-X-LLM , a video language model fine-tuned for facial video understanding. We build on InternVideo2.5 [ 38 ] and adapt it to the face domain by fine-tuning on ExplainFace with Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) training. Fig. 1 shows the architecture. Base Model Details. InternVideo2.5 [ 38 ] has three parts: a vision encoder, a vision language connector, and a language decoder. The vision encoder follows InternViT: 24 24 transformer layers, hidden size 1024 1024 , 16 16 heads. It reads frames at 448 × 448 448\times 448 with patch size 14 14 , and uses Flash Attention [ 12 ] for speed. The connector is a two-layer MLP with 0.5 0.5 downsampling that maps visual features into the language space. The decoder is InternLM2.5-7B [ 7 ] : 32 32 layers, hidden size 4096 4096 , group-query attention with 32 32 heads and 8 8 key/value heads. Fine-tuning Details. We train on the question answer pairs from ExplainFace ( Sec. 3 ) with the matching CelebV-HQ videos. We fine-tune end-to-end to predict the answer, using FSDP [ 48 ] .

sections.text: Video language models [ 18 , 39 ] are strong, but their deep encoders and cross-modal attention make it hard to say which region or moment drove a prediction. We address this with H-TCC, which finds when a key event happens, where the model looks, and why that evidence is needed ( Fig. 2 ). Problem definition. Given a video V = { f 1 , … , f T } V=\{f_{1},\dots,f_{T}\} and a predicted attribute a a , H-TCC returns a temporal peak t ⋆ t^{\star} ( When ), a spatial attention map R R over image patches ( Where ), and a necessity decision ( Why ). We call an explanation faithful if perturbing the identified evidence changes the prediction more than perturbing random evidence. Figure 2 : Overview of H-TCC. Phase 1 detects the peak moment ( When ); Phase 2 localises where the model attends on the face ( Where ); Phase 3 tests whether that evidence is needed ( Why ). See Sec. 5 . Textual Attention: we read the model’s natural-language explanation, run symmetric rollout over the language layers, and find attribute-specific phrases from a small evidence vocabulary. Their influence on the attribute token gives a ranked list of supporting evidence. For emotion, we do this per segment with segment-specific text. Phase 3: Necessity Validation via Targeted Occlusion (Why). The first two phases tell us when and where the model’s evidence lies; Phase 3 confirms that this evidence is actually necessary for the prediction, rather than merely present alongside it. We test necessity directly through targeted occlusion: we apply a strong Gaussian blur to the specific evidence identified by Phases 1 and 2, and use VideoFace-X-LLM itself to check whether the target attribute is still detected after masking. Because the evidence is already localised in time and space, the test is far cheaper and easier to read than blind occlusion over the whole input. Temporal validation. For each predicted attribute, we take the peak frame identified in Phase 1, apply a strong blur to it, and check whether the model still predicts the attribute. We repeat this for randomly selected frames from the same clip. A peak frame is judged causally important if blurring it changes the prediction more often than blurring a random frame. We summarise this as a causal score: the ratio of the peak-frame impact to the average random-frame impact, where a score above 1.0 1.0 means the identified moment matters more than chance. Spatial validation. We validate the Phase 2 attention regions the same way. We blur the top 10 % 10\% highest-attention patches in the peak frame and check whether the attribute prediction changes, then blur random regions of equal area for comparison. A causal score above 1.0 1.0 indicates the highlighted region is necessary rather than incidental. We use the term causal in the sense of a controlled intervention test, blur the evidence and measure the effect which establishes that the identified evidence is needed for the prediction; it confirms necessity rather than recovering the model’s full internal reasoning. sections.heading: 6 Experiments
sections.text: Tasks, Datasets, and Metrics. We evaluate VideoFace-X-LLM on six tasks. Appearance Attributes: the model predicts visual attributes such as facial features, hair, and accessories. This uses CelebV-HQ [ 50 ] as a 40 40 -class multi-label task. We report Mean Accuracy (mA) and Macro F1 . mA averages per-attribute accuracy; Macro F1 handles the imbalance of rare attributes. Action Attributes: the model predicts facial actions such as talking, laughing, or singing, on CelebV-HQ [ 50 ] as a 35 35 -class multi-label task. We report mA and Macro F1, as for appearance. Emotion Recognition: we use two settings. At the video level the model predicts the dominant emotion over the whole clip from eight classes (neutral, happy, sad, anger, fear, disgust, surprise, contempt). We report accuracy and Macro F1 for both the video and temporal settings. Facial Deepfake: the model predicts whether a face is real or manipulated, on FaceForensics++ [ 31 ] . This is binary; we report accuracy and F1. Action Units (AUs): Action Units are the basic facial-muscle movements defined by the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) [ 15 ] . We evaluate on DISFA [ 24 ] , which gives frame-level intensity for eight AUs; we treat an AU as active if intensity ≥ 2 \geq 2 . We report Macro F1 at clip and frame level, plus mA at clip level. Note on data. We fine-tune on CelebV-HQ videos paired with Gemini descriptions. As CelebV-HQ has no official train/test split, we build an identity-independent one by grouping clips by face identity (ArcFace [ 13 ] embeddings) and by source YouTube video and assigning whole groups to one split ( 80 % 80\% train, 20 % 20\% test), so all CelebV-HQ evaluations are on unseen identities and videos. Deepfake (FaceForensics++) and Action Units (DISFA) are entirely separate datasets, so they test cross-dataset transfer. Training Configurations. We try two settings. ViT-Only: we freeze the language model, and train only the vision encoder and the connector, so the encoder adapts to faces while the language model stays fixed. LLM+ViT: we train all parts (encoder, connector, language model) together. Implementation Details. We use the XTuner framework on PyTorch, with 2 2 NVIDIA A100 GPUs and FSDP full sharding. Each GPU uses micro-batch size 1 1 with gradient accumulation. We train for 1 1 epoch, global batch size 16 16 , learning rate 4 × 10 − 5 4\times 10^{-5} for all parts, weight decay 0.01 0.01 , 3 % 3\% linear warmup then cosine decay, AdamW with gradient clipping at norm 1.0 1.0 , and 8 8 frames per video. For all tasks the model returns structured JSON, compared against CelebV-HQ ground truth. We compare against off-the-shelf MLLMs (MiniCPM-V [ 40 ] , InternVL, Qwen-VL [ 39 , 5 ] , LLaVA-NeXT [ 46 ] , Phi-4 [ 2 ] ) using their public code.

In Phase 1, the saliency is high only in a few short time windows, not spread over the whole video, so the model picks out the moments that matter. In Phase 2 (target black hair ), the model looks at the hair region and ignores the background. In Phase 3, blurring this evidence drops the prediction; blurring other parts does not.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduce VideoFace-X-LLM, a facial video language model fine-tuned on the weakly labeled ExplainFace corpus, learning spatio-temporal features that transfer to emotion, deepfake, Action Unit, and attribute tasks. Broader Impact. It can serve as a base model for facial video analysis in affective computing, HCI, and behaviour understanding. Limitations. The model can inherit demographic bias from CelebV-HQ and preprocessing, and MLLMs can hallucinate; future work will add more diverse data. Acknowledgements. Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.17791v1 [cs.CV] 13 Oct 2026 When, Where, and Why: Hierarchical Causal Explainability for Video Face Understanding with MLLMs Anubhav Kataria Affiliation: Monash University, Melbourne, Australia Shreya Ghosh Affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur, Kharagpur, India Jingwen Ye Affiliation: Monash University, Melbourne, Australia Abhinav Dhall Affiliation: Monash University, Melbourne, Australia Abstract Understanding facial behaviour in video requires answering three fundamental questions: when a key facial expression occurs, where the model attends on the face at that moment, and why that evidence is necessary rather than merely correlated. Today’s multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can label and describe video, but they rarely provide faithful explanations, especially for small facial movements that change over time. We present VideoFace-X-LLM , a framework for explainable facial video understanding comprising two key components. First, we introduce ExplainFace , a weakly supervised video-text corpus for facial behaviour understanding, automatically constructed from CelebV-HQ videos and validated through human evaluation and a two-model audit (at most 2.3% contradictions), demonstrating consistent gains across two backbone architectures. Second, H-TCC (Hierarchical Temporal Spatial Causal Concepts), which finds the key temporal moments ( When ), the facial regions ( Where ), and verifies its causal necessity ( Why ) through targeted occlusion. Fine-tuning on ExplainFace raises appearance Macro F1 from 19.48 % 19.48\% to 32.87 % 32.87\% ( + 13.39 +13.39 ), with gains of + 4.38 +4.38 on actions, + 6.77 +6.77 on temporal emotion, and + 11.84 +11.84 F1 on deepfake detection. We also measure the explanations pointing lift, face/edge lift, stability, an Adebayo sanity check, and a necessity test rather than only showing examples. Our models, code, and corpus are available on request for research use. Keywords: Facial Foundational Model Explainability Spatio-Temporal Analysis Figure 1 : Overview of VideoFace-X-LLM. Left: the ExplainFace corpus is built by prompting Gemini for multi-aspect video descriptions, then auditing them for quality and bias. Top: the MLLM is fine-tuned on this corpus. Right: H-TCC explains each prediction by finding when the key moment occurs, where the model looks on the face, and why that evidence is needed. 1 Introduction Faces in motion are one of the richest signals of human behaviour. A raised brow becomes surprise only when we see it change over time; a smile becomes warmth or sarcasm depending on the gaze, head motion, voice, and context around it. Such behaviour is temporal, multimodal, and causal: meaning comes not from single frames, but from how visual and audio signals change together. To understand it well, a model should answer three questions: when a key event happens, where it shows on the face at that moment, and why that region is needed and not just present by chance. The three are linked: a good explanation must find the right moment and region, then confirm that this evidence drives the output. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have improved fast on general vision language tasks, but they are still weak at fine-grained facial behaviour. Existing MLLMs [ 18 , 39 ] are trained on broad data and lack the priors needed to read small facial motions, micro-expression changes, and cues that depend on time but they remain strong at open-ended video description and soft-labeling. This is even harder for explanation, where a model must justify a prediction over time , not just describe a still image. Recent models such as InternVideo2.5 [ 38 ] , GPT-4o [ 26 ] , and Qwen3-VL [ 39 ] are strong at captioning, VQA, and general video analysis, yet they struggle with human-centric reasoning. Their training data is broad but thin on detailed labels for expressions, affect, body language, and temporal change. The real problem is not the models but the data: there is no large video-text dataset that describes faces in detail and lines up those descriptions with time. Weakly supervised, language-model-based dataset building has been tried for still images (for example FaceLLM’s FairFaceGPT [ 33 ] ), but not for video. Moving from images to video is harder, because it needs grounding of facial attributes in both space and time, plus reasoning over small changes that unfold over time. We address this with VideoFace-X-LLM , a model for explainable facial behaviour in video. We build ExplainFace , a weakly supervised video text corpus generated with Gemini [ 18 ] , giving time-aligned descriptions of facial attributes, expression dynamics, and audio visual context. To explain predictions, we introduce H-TCC (Hierarchical Temporal Spatial Causal Concepts), which finds when key events occur, where the model looks on the face, and why that evidence is needed, using hierarchical temporal saliency, spatial attribution, and a targeted occlusion test that confirms the identified evidence is necessary for the prediction. Importantly, fine-tuning on ExplainFace helps two different backbones, and we measure the explanations rather than only showing examples. Our main contributions are: • ExplainFace: a checked, weakly-labeled dataset. We label CelebV-HQ videos using Gemini instead of expensive frame-by-frame human labeling. We test how good these labels are with two human studies and a two-model check for bias, and show the labels still work well when used with two different model backbones. • H-TCC: a when/where/why framework that we actually measure. Every step of H-TCC is defined with clear equations, and we score the explanations with quantitative faithfulness metrics (pointing/face/edge lifts, stability, a sanity check, and a necessity test), not just example cases. • VideoFace-X-LLM. A video-understanding model for faces that explains its answers by pointing to the exact moments and regions that led to its decision. 2 Related Work MLLMs for Vision Language Understanding. Recent MLLMs such as GPT-4o [ 26 ] , InternVideo2.5 [ 38 ] , LLaVA-NeXT [ 46 ] , and Qwen3-VL [ 39 ] have pushed general image and video reasoning, but lack the domain priors and time-aligned supervision needed for subtle facial behaviour, motivating our specialised corpus and adapted MLLM. Human-Centric Facial Behaviour Understanding. Many works apply MLLMs and foundation models to faces: recognition [ 13 ] , attribute analysis [ 23 ] , understanding [ 9 ] , and multimodal reasoning [ 11 ] . A recent survey [ 34 ] reviews how foundation models and LLMs are used for biometric security. Beyond CLIP, self-supervised methods learn facial representations, such as the masked-autoencoder MARLIN [ 8 ] , FaRL [ 49 ] , DINO-style distillation [ 6 ] , and ComFace [ 4 ] . Multi-task models [ 25 ] jointly do face parsing, landmarks, pose, and attributes. HumanOmni [ 47 ] uses a dedicated face branch and does well on expression and emotion. Still, no existing work gives both time-aligned video labels and clear, trustworthy explanations which is what VideoFace-X-LLM sets out to do. Bias and Explainability for Facial Behaviour Understanding. Facial datasets carry demographic imbalance that flows into predictions, with uneven results across gender, race, and age [ 14 ] . LLMs can amplify such bias when describing faces [ 17 ] , and bias checks for video face descriptions are still missing. 1) Temporal Explainability ( When ). Several methods [ 43 , 41 , 20 ] find key moments in video. TimeSuite [ 43 ] adds temporal grounding, SeViLA [ 41 ] picks keyframes, and VTimeLLM [ 20 ] and TimeChat [ 30 ] encode timestamps as text. Grounded-VideoLLM [ 36 ] splits video into spatial and temporal tokens. However, looking at only one time scale can miss events that overlap. 2) Spatial Explainability ( Where ). Grad-CAM [ 32 ] makes spatial heatmaps from gradients but does not suit transformer encoders or video. For vision transformers, attention rollout [ 1 ] traces information across layers, with refinements that mix gradients and attention [ 10 ] . GMAR [ 21 ] reweights heads by gradient importance, and LVLM-Interpret [ 35 ] extends rollout to large models. However, these maps do not line up with time. 3) Causal Validation ( Why ). Occlusion methods test whether evidence is needed by masking inputs and watching the output change. Zeiler and Fergus [ 42 ] used systematic occlusion for CNNs, RISE [ 28 ] uses random masks, and Fong and Vedaldi [ 16 ] frame it as finding the smallest change that flips the output. The problem is that they perturb blindly, without knowing when or where to look, which is slow and hard to read. They are also not built for video MLLMs, where masks must cover both time and space. Existing methods usually answer only one of when , where , or why , each with limits that our H-TCC addresses together. 3 ExplainFace Corpus Most MLLMs [ 38 , 39 ] are trained on broad data with little human-centric detail, so they miss subtle facial behaviour and affect over time. We close this gap with ExplainFace , a video text corpus for detailed analysis of faces over time. We use videos from CelebV-HQ [ 50 ] and generate descriptions with the Gemini API [ 18 ] . The pipeline has two stages: a system prompt for video analysis (Prompt 3.1) followed by a multi-aspect description prompt; then a bias audit of those descriptions (Prompt 3.2). Because the model can answer in different ways for different videos, we use a fixed system prompt (Prompt 3.1) so the output stays detailed and structured. Multi-Aspect Description Generation. For each video we generate descriptions over eight aspects: theme & narrative, visual elements, actions & movements, audio components, emotional tone, technical aspects, temporal flow, and context & relationships . So we add a bias-audit stage that checks each description. A separate prompt asks the model to flag biased language and suggest a neutral version grounded in what is visible. This makes the descriptions both detailed and objective. Subjectivity Audit. Descriptions can go beyond what is visible. A model might call a neutral face ‘reserved’ , or read ‘frustration’ from a raised brow. These are not wrong, but they are interpretations shaped by priors. To measure how much interpretive language is in ExplainFace, we use a two-stage audit. Stage 1: A prompt (Prompt 3.2) reviews each description with its video. For every interpretive statement, the model returns: (i) the exact phrase, (ii) why it goes beyond what is seen, and (iii) a more grounded alternative. If nothing is flagged, it says the description is purely observational. Example flagged pair. For one clip, the draft said the person “looks aggressive .” The audit flagged this as a guess about character and suggested “the brows are drawn together and the jaw is tense” - keeping the visible cue but dropping the assumption. Observations from Stage 1: We run the audit with two models: Gemini 2.5 Flash [ 18 ] and Qwen3-30B-Instruct [ 39 ] . Gemini calls about 70 % 70\% of descriptions observational and 30 % 30\% interpretive; Qwen3 calls about 60 % 60\% observational and 40 % 40\% interpretive. The gap shows the task is fuzzy: even two LLMs disagree on where observation ends and interpretation begins. This supports our view that objectivity in facial description is a spectrum, not a yes/no. Stage 2: Next we compare each flagged phrase with its suggested alternative. The two should keep the same meaning but change the framing. Phase 3: Necessity Validation via Targeted Occlusion (Why). The first two phases tell us when and where the model’s evidence lies; Phase 3 confirms that this evidence is actually necessary for the prediction, rather than merely present alongside it. Because the evidence is already localised in time and space, the test is far cheaper and easier to read than blind occlusion over the whole input. Temporal validation. For each predicted attribute, we take the peak frame identified in Phase 1, apply a strong blur to it, and check whether the model still predicts the attribute. We repeat this for randomly selected frames from the same clip. A peak frame is judged causally important if blurring it changes the prediction more often than blurring a random frame. A causal score above 1.0 1.0 indicates the highlighted region is necessary rather than incidental. We use the term causal in the sense of a controlled intervention test, blur the evidence and measure the effect which establishes that the identified evidence is needed for the prediction; it confirms necessity rather than recovering the model’s full internal reasoning. Appearance Attributes: the model predicts visual attributes such as facial features, hair, and accessories. This uses CelebV-HQ [ 50 ] as a 40 40 -class multi-label task. We report Mean Accuracy (mA) and Macro F1 . mA averages per-attribute accuracy; Macro F1 handles the imbalance of rare attributes. Action Attributes: the model predicts facial actions such as talking, laughing, or singing, on CelebV-HQ [ 50 ] as a 35 35 -class multi-label task. We report mA and Macro F1, as for appearance. Emotion Recognition: we use two settings. At the video level the model predicts the dominant emotion over the whole clip from eight classes (neutral, happy, sad, anger, fear, disgust, surprise, contempt). We report accuracy and Macro F1 for both the video and temporal settings. Facial Deepfake: the model predicts whether a face is real or manipulated, on FaceForensics++ [ 31 ] . This is binary; we report accuracy and F1. Action Units (AUs): Action Units are the basic facial-muscle movements defined by the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) [ 15 ] . We evaluate on DISFA [ 24 ] , which gives frame-level intensity for eight AUs; we treat an AU as active if intensity ≥ 2 \geq 2 . We report Macro F1 at clip and frame level, plus mA at clip level.
